title: RealEstateHub
text:
RealEstateHub is a web platform where sellers can list properties and buyers can browse them and make offers. It is a Java project built with Jakarta EE.
Code on Github

What you can do
There are two kinds of users and each one has their own pages:

Sellers can add and edit properties, see all their listings and accept or reject the offers they receive.

Buyers can search properties, make offers and follow the status of their offers.

Both have a login, a registration page and account settings. When the status of an offer changes, the buyer and the seller get an email through the Brevo API.


How it is built
The project is split in three parts:

Domain model: plain Java classes like Property, Buyer, Seller, Offer and Message, with JUnit tests.

Web service: a REST API with /buyers, /sellers and /offers resources.

Web application: the pages, written with JSF (.xhtml) and backing beans.

Everything runs in Docker with a MySQL database and a Payara server:
services:
  mysql:
    image: mysql:8.0
  payara:
    image: payara/server-full:6.2025.8-jdk17
    depends_on:
      mysql:
        condition: service_healthy
To try it, build the two .war files with Maven and run docker compose up. Payara picks up the apps automatically.

title: Binning
text:
When we have a big dataset and we want to make the analysis easier we can use the binning which is basically classifying the data into the number of bins we want. The number of bins depend on the analysis you’re performing.

Application
To apply this technique we will be using the command cut("dataset", "number of bins", labels = "names of the bins")
It is fairly straight forward to use.
You can use assign this as a variable and then use it to make barplots, graphs, etc..
For example, in one of my assignments we were trying to see the correlation between grades and the mother’s education and we applied the binning to the grades. We classed them into 4 bins and then using the code below we created a ggplot which helps us analyse.
library(ggplot2)
ggplot() +
geom_bar( data = my_data,
aes( x = factor(medu),
fill = factor( G3 ) ),
position = "stack" ) +
scale_x_discrete( "medu" ) +
scale_y_continuous( "G3" ) +
guides( fill = guide_legend( title = "Grades" ) )
ggplot() +
geom_bar( data = my_data,
aes( x = factor(medu),
fill = factor( G3 ) ),
position = "fill" ) +
scale_x_discrete( "medu" ) +
scale_y_continuous( "G3" ) +
guides( fill = guide_legend( title = "Grades" ))

title: IoT Weather Station
text:
For the Cloud and Advanced Analytics course at UNIL HEC, my teammate Zéa and I built an indoor/outdoor weather monitor. It runs on an M5Stack Core2, stores its readings in Google Cloud, and has a live dashboard that you can chat with.
▶️ Demo video on YouTube · Code on Github

How it works
The device reads temperature, humidity, eCO₂ and TVOC from its sensors and sends them to a Flask API running on Cloud Run. The API saves everything in BigQuery and fetches the outdoor weather from OpenWeatherMap. A Streamlit dashboard then reads the data straight from BigQuery.
M5Stack Core2  --HTTP/JSON-->  Flask middleware (Cloud Run)  --SQL-->  BigQuery
                                  • OpenWeatherMap                        |
                                  • Google Maps Geolocation               v
                                  • Google TTS / STT            Streamlit dashboard
                                  • Vertex AI (Gemini)          (Cloud Run)


The device
The M5Stack has a 4 page touch screen and you swipe between the pages:

Page 0: indoor and outdoor temperature and humidity

Page 1: air quality (CO₂, TVOC, AQI, PM2.5, NO₂…)

Page 2: a 5 day forecast

Page 3: a voice assistant

Some of my favourite features:

Voice assistant: tap the screen and ask a question. The recording goes through Google Speech-to-Text, Gemini answers it and the answer is played back with Text-to-Speech.

Rain reminder: in the morning it says “Take an umbrella!” when rain is forecast.

Presence detection: a PIR sensor notices when someone walks by and the device reads out the weather.

WiFi geolocation: the device scans nearby WiFi networks and sends them to the Google Maps Geolocation API to find out where it is, so the outdoor weather is always for the right place.

WiFi setup wizard: an on-screen keyboard to connect to a new network.



My part
I set up the project structure and wrote the middleware API (Flask routes, BigQuery, the voice pipeline and geolocation). On the device I did the firmware logic: NTP time sync, the PIR sensor, sleep and backlight, retry logic, the WiFi wizard and the voice page. I also built the AI chat on the dashboard and did the security hardening.


Dashboard
The dashboard has a live page with gauges, outdoor weather, AQI, UV index and the forecast, plus an analytics page with historical charts. At the bottom there is an AI chat where you can ask things like “What’s the weather in Tokyo?” or “What was the CO₂ yesterday?” and it answers with the live sensor data and the history from BigQuery.

title: Github
text:
Github
Git is an open source software used to keep up with the changes in files and to colaborate between programmers. Here are some basic commands for git:
git add. Usage: git add [file] . . .
git commit. Usage: git commit -m “[ Type in the commit message].


Create a repository in Github
create a folder using mkdirand “name” it then use cd+ “name” to change the directory. Once in the directory run git init and exlplore all the files and folder git.


Create an empty file
Create a new file using touch“name”.txt and using vim “name”.txt write some information.


New repositry in Github
Create a new repositry in Github “name” and make sure it is public.


Public key/ Private key
We will generate our key using ssh-keygen -t ed25519 then we leave this directory using cd. To read our key we us cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub then copy the key and paste it under New SSH key in SSH and GPG key in the GitHub settings give it a “name” and create it.


Upload to new repo
Use cd cloud/project/name to get into your directory and then use git add . to uplaod. Next you will be using git config --global user.email "your_email@example.com". Then use git commit -m + ”name”“ and finally use git push origin master to upload it to Github. If it shows that the there is an error in uploading to the gihub using git push origin master then you can override and forcefully upload by using git push origin master -f.

title: Cleaning supermarket data with tidyr
text:
In this case study we got a supermarket dataset where every row is one customer and every cell is one item they scanned at the till. Each scan looks like “10 24 1.09”, which is the department, the time and the price all squeezed together. To analyse it we first need to tidy it up.
Code on Github

Give the columns names
The raw file has no headers, so I named the columns Item_1, Item_2, … and added a Customer_ID for each row.
library(tidyverse)
data <- read.csv("supermarket.csv")
sampled_data <- data[1:50, ]

colnames(sampled_data) <- paste0("Item_", 1:ncol(sampled_data))

sampled_data <- mutate(Customer_ID = row_number(), sampled_data)


From wide to long
With pivot_longer every scan gets its own row, then the empty cells are removed.
sampled_data <- sampled_data %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("Item"),
               names_to = "Item",
               values_to = "Scan") %>%
  arrange(Customer_ID) %>%
  group_by(Customer_ID) %>%
  filter(!is.na(Scan) & Scan != "")


Split the scan
Finally substring splits the scan into three proper columns that we can use for the analysis.
sampled_data <- sampled_data %>%
  mutate(Department = substring(Scan, 1, 3),
         Time = as.integer(substring(Scan, 4, 6)),
         Price = as.numeric(substring(Scan, 7)))
Now the data has one row per item with the customer, department, time and price, which makes it easy to group, summarise and plot.

title: My Google Code-in R projects
text:
In 2019 I took part in Google Code-in and did a series of tasks for the R Project for Statistical Computing. Here is a quick tour of them.

Reading and writing CSV data
My first task was about reading a CSV into a data frame, adding rows and columns and writing it back out. You can even read a CSV straight from the internet. Code
T2 = data.frame(name = c("Nikhil","Roja","Jitendra","Diksha","Krishna"),
                age = c(17,30,21,28,35),
                class = c("2M1","2M2","2M3","2M4","2M5"))
T2$Height = c(140,180,130,120,130)
write.csv(T2, "students.csv")

X = read.csv("https://archive.ics.uci.edu/ml/machine-learning-databases/iris/iris.data", header = FALSE)
head(X)


Exploring e-commerce data
With dplyr I explored an e-commerce dataset with 1594 observations and 45 variables. Brisbane had the most visitors among the Australian cities. Code
library(dplyr)
subset(ecommerce, country == "Australia") %>%
  group_by(city) %>%
  summarise(behavNumVisits = sum(behavNumVisits)) %>%
  arrange(desc(behavNumVisits))


3D scatter plot with Lattice
The cloud function from lattice makes a 3D scatter plot. Code
library(lattice)
Lattice_data = data.frame(w = c(16,90,46,30), x = c(5,10,20,40),
                          y = c(23,89,66,48), z = c("a","b","c","d"))
cloud(w ~ x * y, groups = Lattice_data$z, Lattice_data)



Interactive plot with animint2
Using the WorldBank data I plotted life expectancy against fertility rate in 1975 and turned it into an interactive chart that I published as a gist. Code
library(animint2)
data(WorldBank, package = "animint2")
WorldBank1975 = subset(WorldBank, year == 1975)
scatter = ggplot() +
  geom_point(mapping = aes(x = life.expectancy, y = fertility.rate, color = region),
             data = WorldBank1975)
animint2gist(animint(scatter))



R package downloads in 2018
The cranlogs API tells you how many times R packages were downloaded. With jsonlite I pulled the totals for 2018, and also for each half of the year, and saved them as CSV. Code
library(jsonlite)
Data = fromJSON("https://cranlogs.r-pkg.org/downloads/total/2018-01-01:2018-12-31")
write.csv(Data, "Data.csv")


A hexagon logo for an R package
Every good R package needs a hex sticker! The hexSticker package makes one from any image. Code
library(hexSticker)
sticker("IMG_0039.png", package = "", p_size = 8,
        s_x = 1, s_y = 1, s_width = .6, filename = "aa.png")

title: CineMatch: a movie recommender
text:
CineMatch is a movie recommendation web app I built for an assignment in the Cloud and Advanced Analytics course. You pick a few movies you like and it suggests what to watch next.
Live app · Code on Github

How it is built
The app has two parts and both run in Docker containers on Google Cloud Run:

Backend (Flask): a REST API that talks to BigQuery ML, Elasticsearch and the TMDB API.

Frontend (Streamlit): the page where you search, filter and pick your movies.



Features

Autocomplete search with Elasticsearch (match_phrase_prefix)

Filters for genre, language, country, year and rating

Posters, overview and cast from the TMDB API

Recommendations from a BigQuery ML matrix factorisation model



How the recommendations work
First I look for users who liked the same movies as you. A movie counts as “liked” if the user gave it at least 0.7 (ratings are scaled from 0 to 1). The more of your movies a user liked, the more similar they are to you.
SELECT userId, COUNT(*) AS common_count
FROM ratings
WHERE movieId IN (<selected_ids>) AND rating_im >= 0.7
GROUP BY userId
ORDER BY common_count DESC
LIMIT 10
Those 10 users are passed to ML.RECOMMEND. Each user’s predicted ratings are weighted by their common_count, so the users closest to you have more say. Finally, movies that share genres with the ones you picked get a boost of 1 + 0.5 × number of shared genres.
score(m) = [ Σ_u  r̂(u,m) · w_u ] / [ Σ_u  w_u ]  ×  genre_boost(m)
